shots.src: World Bank (to 2024) · IMF WEO Oct 2026 (2026) · GDP per capita, PPP
shots.title: Output per person, 1990
shots.narration: In 1990, the average person in Poland produced about six thousand dollars of value a year. {p} The average person in Japan? {pp} Twenty thousand.

shots.src: World Bank · inflation, consumer prices
shots.narration: Poland was coming out of forty years of communism. Inflation was over five hundred percent. Shops had queues, but not much on the shelves. {p} Japan was the second-largest economy on Earth.

shots.src: World Bank (to 2024) · IMF WEO Oct 2026 (2026) · GDP per capita, PPP
shots.narration: Thirty-six years later, the IMF put out a forecast that almost nobody read. {p} In 2026, for the first time ever, {pp} the average Pole out-produces the average Japanese.

Nobody threw a party. Most people didn't notice. {p} This is the story of how a country that was poorer than Ukraine became richer than Japan. {p} <soft>And why the number that explains how it happened... is the same number that could undo it.</soft> Let's go through the chart.

shots.src: World Bank (to 2024) · IMF WEO Oct 2026 (2026) · GDP per capita, PPP · Poland as % of Japan
shots.narration: Here's where the line starts. Thirty percent. That's Poland's income as a share of Japan's, in 1990. And honestly, thirty was generous.

shots.title: 1 January 1990
shots.narration: In 1989, Solidarity won the first partly free election in the Soviet bloc. Months later, on January first, 1990, Poland did something economists still argue about. It ripped the bandage off. {p} Price controls: gone. Subsidies to state factories: gone. The currency: let it float, let it fall. They called it shock therapy. {pp} The shock part was real.

shots.src: World Bank · CPI inflation; unemployment (ILO)
shots.title: Year one of shock therapy
shots.narration: Prices rose more than five hundred percent in a single year. Output fell. Unemployment went from officially zero, because communism didn't admit it existed, to double digits.

shots.src: Paris Club agreement, April 1991
shots.title: A rare break
shots.narration: Poland also got a break that most countries never get. {p} In 1991, the governments it owed money to agreed to forgive half of that debt.

shots.src: World Bank · real GDP growth, Poland
shots.narration: But watch the line. By 1992, Poland was growing again. And here is the stat that actually matters: from 1992 to 2019, Poland's economy grew every single year. Twenty-eight years. {p} No other country in the European Union can say that. Japan, over the same stretch, shrank in seven of those years.
So how do you go from bread lines to no recessions? {p} Three things. And the first one has a date.
May first, 2004. Poland joins the European Union, and the slope of this chart changes.

shots.src: SGH Warsaw School of Economics · EU budget flows 2004–2023 · GDDKiA road network
shots.narration: One: money. Over the next twenty years, Poland becomes the biggest net recipient of EU funds in the whole bloc. Roads, rail, water, broadband. In 2004, Poland had under eight hundred kilometers of motorways and expressways. By 2025, almost five and a half thousand. {p} All told, more than a hundred and sixty billion euros more than it paid in.

shots.src: Statistics Poland (GUS) · exports by destination, 2025
shots.narration: Two: factories. German companies needed somewhere nearby to build parts, with skilled workers and lower costs. Warsaw is a six-hour drive from Berlin. Even Toyota builds engines there. {p} Today, more than a quarter of everything Poland exports goes to Germany.

stats.label: of Polish exports go to Germany

shots.narration: Three: people. Around two million Poles left to work abroad, mostly in Britain and Ireland. They sent money home. {p} And then, slowly, a lot of them came back, with skills and savings.

shots.src: World Bank (to 2024) · IMF WEO Oct 2026 (2026) · GDP per capita, PPP
shots.narration: Look at the slope after 2004. {p} That's not luck. That's a supply chain.

shots.src: World Bank · real GDP growth, 2009
shots.narration: And then 2008. The global financial crisis. In 2009, every single economy in the European Union shrank. {p} Every one, {pp} except Poland. It grew. The press called it the green island. One green dot on a map of red.

shots.title: Why it held
shots.narration: Why? Boring reasons, which are the best reasons. Banks that hadn't gone crazy. A currency, the zloty, that dropped about thirty percent and made Polish exports cheap at exactly the right moment. {p} And a home market of thirty-eight million people buying Polish stuff.

shots.src: World Bank · unemployment rate (ILO)
shots.narration: Look at unemployment. 2002: twenty percent. One in five workers. {p} 2024: under three. {pp} That's not a recovery. That's a different country.

shots.src: World Bank · GDP per capita, PPP
shots.narration: And if you think that's just geography, look next door. {p} In 1990, Ukraine was actually a bit richer than Poland. Similar factories, similar size, same Soviet past. {p} By 2013, before any war, Poland was more than twice as rich. Today, it's nearly three times.

shots.src: World Bank (to 2024) · IMF WEO Oct 2026 (2026) · GDP per capita, PPP
shots.narration: But a crossover has two lines. And the second one barely moved.

shots.src: World Bank (to 2024) · IMF WEO Oct 2026 (2026) · GDP per capita, PPP
shots.narration: In 1990, Japan's bubble popped. Stocks, land, everything. What followed got a name: the Lost Decade. Then the second Lost Decade. {p} In purchasing-power terms, Japan did grow, slowly. From twenty thousand to about fifty-four. {p} Poland went from six... to fifty-one.

shots.src: World Bank · population ages 15–64, Japan
shots.narration: And underneath, something slower was happening. {p} Japan's working-age population peaked in the mid-nineties, and it has been shrinking ever since. {p} Remember that. It comes back.

shots.src: World Bank · GDP per capita, current US$
shots.narration: And in plain dollars, it's worse. In 2012, the average Japanese income was almost fifty thousand dollars. In 2024? {pp} Thirty-four. That's not Japan getting poorer at home. {p} That's the yen losing nearly half its value against the dollar.

shots.src: IMF WEO Oct 2026 · general government gross debt, % of GDP
shots.title: Meanwhile in Tokyo
shots.narration: To keep things moving, Tokyo borrowed. A lot. {p} Japan's government debt is now more than twice the size of its entire economy, the highest in the rich world.
So part of this story is Poland running. {p} <soft>And part of it is Japan standing on an escalator going down.</soft>

items.text: Japan: on an escalator going down

shots.src: World Bank (to 2024) · IMF WEO Oct 2026 (2026) · GDP per capita, PPP
shots.narration: Okay. Poland passes Japan in 2026. {p} Before you move to Warsaw: three catches.

shots.src: OECD · average annual hours worked per worker, 2025
shots.narration: One. Per person is not per hour. Poles work about seventeen hundred and eighty hours a year. The Japanese, about sixteen hundred. {p} That's four and a half extra weeks of full-time work, to make about the same.

shots.src: World Bank · GDP per capita, current US$, 2024
shots.title: In actual dollars, 2024
shots.narration: Two. Purchasing power is not pay. These numbers are adjusted for the fact that a haircut in Krakow costs less than one in Osaka. {p} In actual dollars, Poland's income is still about twenty-five thousand. Japan's, thirty-four.

shots.src: World Bank · fertility rate, births per woman, 2024
shots.title: Babies per woman, 2024
shots.narration: Three. And this is the one. {pp} Babies per woman. Poland, 2024: one point one four. {p} Japan, the country the entire world uses as the example of a shrinking society: {pp} one point one five.
Poland now has fewer children per woman than Japan. {p} Not as few as South Korea, at zero point seven five. {p} But fewer than Japan.

shots.src: World Bank · fertility rate, births per woman
shots.narration: Part of Poland's miracle was a big, young workforce with nowhere to go but up. That workforce is now getting older. {p} Poland's population already peaked, back in the late nineties, and it has been shrinking since. {p} The same math that shrank Japan is already running in Poland. <soft>It just started thirty years later.</soft>

shots.src: World Bank (to 2024) · IMF WEO Oct 2026 (2026) · GDP per capita, PPP
shots.narration: So here's the whole chart, start to finish. Thirty percent of Japan, to a hundred. Along the way, Poland quietly passed Greece, then Portugal. {p} Spain is next: the IMF has the two basically tied this year. {p} Germany? No. Germany is still thirty percent ahead, and the gap isn't closing fast.

But the real question isn't who Poland passes next. It's whether a country can keep climbing after its people stop multiplying. {pp} Japan mostly couldn't. {p} Poland does have a couple of cards Japan never played. Close to a million Ukrainians now live there under temporary protection, and many of them work. And Poland is still catching up, so it can grow by working smarter, not just by adding workers. {p} Will that be enough? Poland is about to find out.

shots.src: World Bank (to 2024) · IMF WEO Oct 2026 (2026) · GDP per capita, PPP
shots.narration: If you'd told someone standing in a Warsaw bread line in 1990 that their grandchildren would out-earn Tokyo... {p} they'd have laughed. {pp} The chart didn't.
If you want the Korea version of this story, the one with the scariest number on Earth, it's right here. {p} I'm Chartbound. See you in the next one.

checks.say: every EU economy shrank except Poland (2009)
South Korea zero point seven five
Poland population peaked in the late nineties
Japan debt more than twice GDP, highest in rich world

yt.title: Poland Just Passed Japan. Nobody Noticed.
yt.description:
For the first time ever, the average Pole out-produces the average Japanese (IMF, GDP per capita at purchasing power, 2026). How Poland went from 30% of Japan to 100% in 36 years, why Japan barely moved, and the number that could undo it all.

Sources: IMF World Economic Outlook (Oct 2026); World Bank WDI (NY.GDP.PCAP.CD, FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG, SL.UEM.TOTL.ZS, NY.GDP.MKTP.KD.ZG, SP.DYN.TFRT.IN, SP.POP.TOTL, PA.NUS.FCRF); OECD hours worked (2025); SGH Warsaw School of Economics, Poland–EU budget flows 2004–2023; Statistics Poland (GUS).
